story.technology: Availability zones can provide distinct infrastructure failure boundaries for redundant application deployments.

title: Bulkhead
lesson: Reserve separate resource pools for different workloads or dependencies. Exhaustion in one pool then leaves capacity for the others, at the cost of sometimes leaving capacity idle.
example: A slow recommendation provider fills its own connection pool. Checkout still has a separate budget to contact payments.
question: Slow image requests consume all worker slots and block account updates. Which design isolates them?
answers: Give image and account work separate bounded worker pools
Expand the single shared queue without a limit
Increase the timeout on every image job
why: A separate pool places a hard boundary on how many slots image work can consume.
detail: Allocate pools around what must survive a failure. Giving each tenant its own queue helps little if every queue drains into a single unbounded shared database pool. Follow requests to the next scarce resource, then enforce a matching admission budget there. Track rejected work by pool to see whether an allocation needs adjusting.

terms.definition: Deciding whether to start new work given current limits.
A separation that limits how a failure or resource shortage spreads.
Isolation of capacity into separate pools so exhaustion of one pool leaves others usable.

story.intro: A slow recommendation service uses up every available worker. Shoppers with items in their baskets still need to pay.
story.meaning: A bulkhead sets aside separate resources for different kinds of work so trouble in one group has a boundary.

steps.label: reserves
steps.caption: It assigns separate workers to suggestions and checkout, with a fixed maximum for each.

steps.label: fill
steps.caption: All suggestion workers are waiting on a slow provider. Additional suggestion requests must wait or fail quickly.

steps.label: serves
steps.caption: The checkout workers are still free to process payments, assuming their own dependencies are healthy.

story.technology: Separate bounded thread or connection pools can isolate independent request paths within one service.

title: Circuit Breaker
lesson: Track failures for a dependency and temporarily stop sending normal calls when the failure threshold is reached. After a cooldown, allow a small trial to test recovery.
example: A map provider times out repeatedly, so the app immediately shows a saved address. While open, the breaker may skip calls that would have succeeded.
question: A provider has timed out for several minutes and each attempt ties up a worker. Which action should an open breaker take?
answers: Fail fast or use a fallback while allowing controlled recovery probes later
Send each new request with several immediate retries
Hold all workers until the provider recovers
why: Failing fast releases local resources. Limited probes discover recovery without flooding the dependency.
detail: Measure enough calls to tell a real outage from a single unlucky request. A breaker can open after a sustained failure rate, wait, then permit a limited number of trial calls. Decide which errors should count. A caller's invalid input usually says little about whether the dependency can serve its next valid request.

terms.definition: The period when a breaker blocks ordinary calls to a dependency.
A trial period when a breaker admits limited calls to evaluate recovery.
A mechanism that temporarily stops calls to a failing dependency and later probes for recovery.

story.intro: A map provider is down. Every delivery order spends ten seconds waiting for a map that never loads.
story.meaning: A circuit breaker remembers repeated dependency failures. It temporarily blocks normal calls and later tests whether the dependency has recovered.

steps.label: observes
steps.caption: The breaker records timeouts until the configured failure threshold is reached.

steps.label: returns
steps.caption: New orders show the saved address promptly. Workers can move on while the map provider recovers.

steps.label: tests
steps.caption: After a cooldown the breaker admits a limited test. A healthy result can allow normal calls again.

story.technology: Resilience4j provides a circuit breaker with closed, open and half-open states for Java applications.

title: Resiliency
lesson: Prepare to recover useful behavior after disruption. Recovery time and recovery point objectives describe how long an interruption may last and how much recent data loss is tolerable.
example: A journal app can restore yesterday's backup quickly, yet still lose a day's entries. More frequent durable copies reduce that gap at extra cost.
question: Your service recovers in five minutes but loses an hour of accepted edits. Which target measures that loss window?
answers: Recovery point objective
Recovery time objective
Median request latency
why: The recovery point objective measures tolerable data loss in time. Recovery time measures how long restoration takes.
detail: Practice restoring into an empty environment and then try opening a real record. A completed backup job alone cannot show that the restored data, schema, credentials and application work together. Time the entire exercise and inspect how recent the last recovered record is. These measurements turn a recovery promise into something the team can test.

terms.definition: A rehearsal that checks whether a recovery procedure produces a usable service.
The latest point in the data history that a recovery procedure restores.

story.intro: A journal app loses its main copy of a notebook. Yesterday's backup exists, but the writer needs this morning's entries too.
story.meaning: Resiliency is the ability to keep useful work going or recover it after disruption. Recovery time and recovered data are separate things to measure.

steps.label: sets
steps.caption: They choose how long restoration may take and how many minutes of recent edits they can afford to lose.

steps.label: restores
steps.caption: The team restores a recent backup into a fresh environment and opens the notebook.

steps.label: compares
steps.caption: They check the entry's time and the total minutes spent restoring. Those measurements show which target needs attention.

story.technology: A scheduled backup plus a timed restore test can verify that a real record is readable after recovery.

title: Compensating Transaction
lesson: When several services commit separate steps, a later failure can require new actions that offset earlier steps. Persist progress and make compensations safe to retry.
example: A rail ticket is booked before a hotel rejects a package. Canceling the ticket may incur a fee, so the compensation follows the actual refund policy.
question: A package purchase fails after a partner has already issued a ticket. How should the workflow recover?
answers: Record and run the partner's cancellation or refund operation
Roll back only the local package database and assume the ticket disappears
Replay the entire purchase with a new booking ID
why: The partner committed independent state. A compensating business action reconciles that state according to the partner's rules.
detail: A refund can be interrupted too. Store a record of which reversals remain and give each one a stable operation ID so a restarted worker can continue safely. Decide which steps require human review, such as a partner refusing cancellation. Show the user a pending resolution state while the system still has business work to complete.

terms.definition: A distributed business workflow composed of local transactions and recovery actions.
A corrective action that can be repeated without applying the correction twice.

story.intro: A travel app books a train, then discovers the guest's hotel is full. The train company has already issued the ticket.
story.meaning: Sometimes the first action has already happened when the next one fails. The travel app can ask the train company to cancel or refund the issued ticket. That follow-up action is called compensation.

steps.label: reserves
steps.caption: The train company confirms a real ticket and returns its reference.

steps.label: declines
steps.caption: The package cannot be completed. The travel app records that the train step needs a follow-up.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: It uses the reference to cancel under the operator's refund policy. It records the outcome so a restart can resume safely.

story.technology: A workflow engine can persist a cancellation step and retry it with a stable reference if the partner is briefly unavailable.

title: Retry
lesson: Repeat an operation after a temporary failure within a deadline and attempt budget. Backoff and jitter spread attempts over time, and a stable operation key can protect side effects.
example: A payment response times out after the bank may have charged the card. Retrying with the same idempotency key lets the provider recognize that payment.
question: A charge request times out with an unknown outcome. What makes a retry safer?
answers: Reuse a provider-supported idempotency key for that charge
Generate a distinct purchase ID on every attempt
Keep retrying instantly until a response arrives
why: The same operation identity lets the provider return or complete the original charge without creating another.
detail: Fit each attempt inside the user's total deadline. If a request has 500 milliseconds left, waiting a full second for a retry cannot help that caller. Classify failures as temporary or permanent, space temporary attempts apart and cap their count. A small randomized delay reduces the chance of thousands of clients trying again at the same instant.

terms.definition: Increasing the delay between successive attempts.
Random variation added to retry timing to spread traffic over time.

story.intro: A shopper presses Pay. The bank may have charged the card, but its reply gets lost.
story.meaning: Retry means making another attempt when a failure might be temporary. Repeated attempts at the same action need a shared identity when money or other side effects are involved.

steps.label: submits
steps.caption: It asks a payment provider that supports duplicate-safe requests to charge the order with key 51.

steps.label: misses
steps.caption: The shopper's connection times out. Checkout still cannot tell whether the provider charged the card.

steps.label: reuses
steps.caption: After a short delay it resends the same operation key. The provider can recognize a completed charge and return its original result.

story.technology: Stripe supports idempotency keys that associate eligible repeated requests with their initial result.

title: Security
lesson: Identify who can call a system, which actions each identity can perform and where sensitive data travels. Apply controls at the point where a protected action takes place.
example: A notes API verifies a signed-in user and checks ownership before reading a private note. That extra lookup protects against exposing another user's note.
question: Two users are signed in. What should the API check before returning a private document by ID?
answers: Whether this user is authorized to read this document
Whether the document ID has a valid format
Whether this user signed in within the past day
why: Authentication identifies the caller. Resource-specific authorization determines whether that caller may read the document.
detail: Start with one valuable action, such as exporting a workspace. Identify the caller, the workspace, the requested operation and where permissions are checked. Record a useful audit event when the export starts, and limit access to the resulting file as well. Protecting the request alone leaves a gap if its output can be fetched by anyone.

terms.definition: An identifiable actor, such as a person or service, whose permissions can be checked.
Granting only the access required for the intended task and duration.

story.intro: A student taps a private notebook link that belongs to another classmate. Both students have valid school accounts.
story.meaning: Security protects information and actions from unauthorized use. A service needs to know both who is asking and what that person is allowed to do.

steps.label: identifies
steps.caption: The notes service verifies the session and obtains the reader's account identity.

steps.label: checks
steps.caption: It compares that identity with the notebook's owner and permitted collaborators.

steps.label: protects
steps.caption: This reader has no entry, so the service refuses access before returning any note text.

story.technology: A server-side authorization check can compare the session identity with a notebook membership table on every read.

title: Federated Identity
lesson: Trust an external identity provider to authenticate a user and issue a verifiable assertion or token. Your service validates the token and decides what the identity may access locally.
example: A university app accepts campus sign-in. Disabling an account at the provider can take time to affect previously issued tokens, depending on their lifetime.
question: A campus login token has a valid signature but names a different application as its audience. What should your app do?
answers: Reject the token because it was issued for another audience
Accept it because both applications trust the campus provider
Use the username alone to create a local session
why: Audience validation binds an assertion to its intended recipient. A valid signature alone does not grant access to every trusting app.
detail: A service can identify a user using both the provider's identity and the user's stable subject identifier. An email address can change or be reassigned and may be ambiguous across providers. Validate the token for the chosen protocol, including its intended audience and lifetime, then map that authenticated identity to permissions in the application.

terms.definition: The authority that created an identity assertion or token.
The identifier the issuer assigns to the user or other principal represented by a token.

story.intro: A student already has a campus account. The library app wants her to use it without collecting her campus password.
story.meaning: Federated identity lets an app trust a separate identity provider to confirm who signed in. The app still decides what that identity may do.

steps.label: redirects to
steps.caption: The student signs in with the campus provider. The library app never needs the campus password.

steps.label: confirms
steps.caption: Through the sign-in flow the library receives a signed identity token intended for this app.

steps.label: opens
steps.caption: It checks the token's issuer, signature, audience and lifetime, then looks up this student's library permissions.

story.technology: OpenID Connect is a sign-in protocol that lets a relying application obtain verified identity information from a provider.

title: Gatekeeper
lesson: Place a controlled entry service in front of a protected backend to check incoming requests. Restrict direct backend access so callers cannot bypass those checks.
example: A file-processing API admits validated requests from a gateway over a private network. The gateway needs its own redundancy to avoid becoming a common failure point.
question: A gateway validates requests, but a backend also accepts direct public calls. What closes this gap?
answers: Restrict backend ingress to the trusted path and authorized callers
Add more validation messages to the gateway response
Increase the cache lifetime of the backend address
why: The protection applies only when requests pass through the enforced checks. Ingress policy makes that boundary effective.
detail: Keep validation at the front door inexpensive enough to apply under load. For a document conversion service, check the caller's permission and allowed request size before assigning a costly conversion worker. The worker still verifies the document conditions it understands. Give the entry service only the access it needs to send accepted jobs onward.

terms.definition: Traffic entering a service or network boundary.
Using several independent protections so one missed check does not expose the entire system.

story.intro: A document converter is expensive to run. Broken or oversized submissions should be stopped before a converter starts.
story.meaning: A gatekeeper is a controlled entry point that checks requests before letting them reach a protected backend.

steps.label: submits
steps.caption: The request first reaches the upload gateway, the only public entry to the service.

steps.label: checks
steps.caption: The gateway verifies the caller and enforces its allowed size. A rejected request never occupies a conversion worker.

steps.label: reaches
steps.caption: Only requests through the trusted route reach the backend. The worker still checks the file format before processing.

story.technology: A gateway with ingress controls and a private worker service can enforce this entry boundary.

title: Valet Key
lesson: After checking permission, issue a short-lived credential scoped to one resource and action. The client can then transfer data directly without routing the bytes through your application.
example: A photo app signs a five-minute upload URL for one object. Anyone holding a usable URL may exercise its permissions until it expires.
question: A user should upload one profile picture directly to storage. Which credential fits?
answers: A short-lived write permission scoped to that user's target object
A permanent account-wide storage key
A read-only link to the whole photo bucket
why: The credential needs just the intended operation, object and time window. Direct transfer keeps the file bytes off the app server.
detail: Choose a unique object name before issuing an upload grant, then verify completion before adding the image to a public gallery. A grant to upload bytes says nothing about whether the resulting image is valid. Keep its expiry long enough for the transfer and short enough to limit exposure if the URL is shared accidentally.

terms.definition: A URL containing a verifiable, scoped grant to perform an operation on a resource.
The time after which a credential is no longer accepted for new requests.

story.intro: A musician needs to upload one new song from her phone. Giving her the studio's storage account credentials would grant far too much access.
story.meaning: A valet key is a temporary credential for one limited job. The client takes it directly to the service holding the resource.

steps.label: requests
steps.caption: The studio app checks that the musician may add a track to this album.

steps.label: issues
steps.caption: The signed link allows an upload to one new object for a short period. The app keeps its broader storage credentials private.

steps.label: uploads to
steps.caption: The song goes directly into storage using the link. The studio can verify the uploaded media before publishing it.

story.technology: An Amazon S3 presigned upload link can authorize a PUT operation for a specific object and expiration time.
